summary.text: 字 is commonly analyzed as a compound showing 子 beneath 宀: a child under a roof. In this interpretation 子 also supplies a sound cue. The early picture is tied to birth and nurture; 字 later commonly means a written character, but the timing and path between these meanings are unresolved. [ref003, ref012, ref024, ref031]

formation.text: Phonosemantic under the traditional analysis: 宀 contributes the setting of a roof or indoor space, while 子 depicts a child and is also assigned a phonetic role. A bronze form is reported with 子 below 宀, but no image was independently inspected and competing analyses are noted. [ref003, ref012, ref015, ref031]

components.text: 宀 is the roof-shaped element above 子. The traditional analysis treats it as semantic, locating the child indoors; its contribution to the proposed original scene is pictorial. [ref001, ref003, ref012]
子 is the child-shaped element below 宀. It depicts the child in the proposed scene and is also assigned a phonetic role by the traditional analysis. [ref001, ref003, ref012]

sound.text: In modern Mandarin, 子 is zǐ and 字 is zì. This is a current reading comparison, not proof of their historical sound relation. [ref013, ref024, ref025]

history.text: A bronze-script form is reported as 子 below 宀, and a catalog lists a Shang-period rubbing associated with 字父己觶. The available record does not verify the specific glyph image, establish its reading in context, or show that it is the earliest attestation. [ref012, ref022, ref023]

The Han lexicographic account glosses 字 as birth or nurture and analyzes it as 子 beneath 宀, with 子 also serving as sound. Later commentary links birth to nurture and then to written characters; this is a transmitted explanation, not a securely dated sequence. [ref003, ref016, ref030]

A research result reports challenges to the traditional graphic analysis, but the underlying discussion was not accessible here, so competing explanations cannot be assessed. The dossier does not establish a graphic corruption or miscopying. [ref031]

uncertainties.text: The dossier supports the traditional 子-under-宀 account and reports scholarly disagreement, but provides no independently inspected paleographic study to resolve the graph’s construction. [ref003, ref012, ref031]

No securely dated early examples establish when 字 meant birth or nurture versus a written character, or whether the latter sense developed from the former or came from a different root. [ref004, ref024, ref030]

The modern Mandarin readings zǐ and zì do not establish the ancient phonetic relation; a local reconstruction dataset proposes a comparison, but its exact entries were not independently verified upstream and do not by themselves prove the graphic analysis. [ref013, ref018, ref019, ref026]

senses.period: Han lexicographic account; earlier dating unresolved
senses.text: The Han account gives birth or nurture as the meaning. The dossier does not establish the date of this sense or whether birth and nurture were one original lexical meaning. [ref003, ref030]
字 commonly means a written character. The dossier does not provide a securely dated earliest example of this sense. [ref012, ref024]
‘Word’ is also listed among the character’s meanings, but the dossier does not establish its chronology or connection to the birth/nurture sense. [ref006, ref024]

developments.text: A later commentary proposes development from birth through nurture to written characters, while another account allows a distinct root or derivation from producing or generating. The dossier does not date or resolve these explanations. [ref004, ref030]

limitations.text: Dictionary glosses and the Han lexicographic explanation do not independently establish the chronology of these senses. [ref017, ref024, ref030]

overview.text: 字 is commonly analyzed as a child (子) beneath a roof (宀), with 子 also serving as a sound cue. The early account links it to birth and nurture; it is now commonly used for a written character. [ref003, ref012, ref024]

components.text: The roof element sets the indoor scene in the traditional interpretation. [ref003, ref012]
The child element appears in the scene; the traditional account also assigns it a sound role. [ref003, ref012]

takeaway.text: The proposed link from birth and nurture to ‘written character’ is an old explanation, but its chronology and development are unresolved. [ref030, ref031]

relationships.text: In the traditional construction, 宀 depicts the roof or indoor setting of the proposed child-under-a-roof scene. [ref003, ref012]
In the traditional construction, 子 depicts the child beneath the roof. [ref001, ref003, ref012]

The traditional analysis assigns 子 a sound role. Modern Mandarin 子 zǐ and 字 zì are a real comparison, but do not establish the ancient relation; a local reconstruction dataset reports a compatible comparison whose exact entries were not independently verified upstream. [ref003, ref013, ref018, ref019, ref025, ref026]
